title: Even Light Exercise Lowers Stroke and Death Risk for People With AFib, Major Study Finds
excerpt: A 15-year study of 87,000 adults found that even low levels of physical activity reduced stroke risk by 9% and extended life by up to 1.2 years for those with atrial fibrillation
body:
• A study of 87,340 adults tracked over 15 years found that even light physical activity was linked to a 9% lower risk of stroke and an 11% lower risk of death from any cause
  • People with atrial fibrillation who stayed active lived up to 1.2 years longer than those who were inactive, with benefits observed at all activity levels
  • The study, published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, found similar benefits whether participants had AFib or not

People with atrial fibrillation — the most common heart rhythm disorder — can significantly reduce their risk of stroke and premature death with even modest amounts of physical activity, according to a large-scale study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association.

The research, which tracked more than 87,000 adults in Norway over approximately 15 years, found that physical activity was associated with reduced stroke risk and longer life regardless of whether participants had atrial fibrillation (AFib). The findings challenge the assumption that people with irregular heartbeats should limit their exercise.

What the Numbers Show

Compared to adults who were inactive, those with low levels of physical activity had a 9% lower risk of stroke. The benefit increased with activity level: moderate activity was linked to a 19% reduction, and high activity to an 18% reduction.

The pattern was similar for mortality. Low, moderate, and high levels of physical activity were associated with 11%, 18%, and 22% lower risks of death from any cause, respectively.

Among adults with AFib specifically, those who remained physically active lived an average of 0.5 to 1.2 years longer than their sedentary counterparts.

"Real health benefits can happen no matter when a person starts getting active, and even a little exercise is better than nothing."

— Kristoffer Johansen, Ph.D., UiT The Arctic University of Norway

Why It Matters for AFib Patients

AFib is a quivering or irregular heartbeat in the heart's upper chambers that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and other serious complications. The condition affects an estimated 10.55 million Americans — about 4.48% of the adult population, according to the American Heart Association's 2026 Heart Disease and Stroke Statistics.

People with AFib tend to be less physically active than the general population, in part because symptoms like heart palpitations, fatigue, and dizziness can make exercise feel risky or uncomfortable. But the study suggests that inactivity may pose a greater danger.

"In general, people with AFib appear to be less active than the general population," said lead study author Kristoffer Johansen, a researcher at the School of Sport Sciences at UiT The Arctic University of Norway. "The results from our study indicate that physical activity was associated with a reduced risk of stroke and death in individuals with and without atrial fibrillation."

Study Design and Limitations

The study drew on data from 87,340 participants in two major Norwegian health research projects: the Tromsø Study and the Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT). Participants had an average age of about 51 at enrollment, roughly 47% were men, and more than 6,500 had AFib at the start of the study or developed it during follow-up.

Researchers classified participants' physical activity into four levels based on self-reported frequency, duration, and intensity, ranging from inactive to highly active. Stroke and death outcomes were tracked through Norway's national health registries.

Because the study was observational rather than a controlled trial, the researchers cannot definitively prove that exercise caused the improved outcomes. More active participants may have been healthier overall, and self-reported activity levels may not be perfectly accurate.

Expert Recommendations

Mina Chung, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic and co-chair of clinical guidelines for AFib management, said the study "adds important evidence linking physical activity with lower risks of stroke and death in people with and without AFib."

The American Heart Association recommends that all adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous aerobic activity per week, along with muscle-strengthening activity at least twice weekly. Experts emphasize that exercise should complement, not replace, standard AFib treatments including medications.
